commons.title: Cascadia State Park, Oregon (39714062044).jpg
commons.credit: Bonnie Moreland from Oregon, United States
commons.description:
Prior to settlers arriving, groups from the Molalla and Kalapuya tribes visited the park site to harvest huckleberries, fish and hunt. Cascadia Cave is nearby. The cave is an 8,000-year-old American Indian petroglyph site considered to have the largest concentration of rock engravings in western Oregon.
Willamette Valley settlers developed a bypass at the park site for horse-drawn wagons. Old wagon ruts are still visible near where Soda Creek meets the South Santiam River.

In 1896, George Geisendorfer opened a resort to capitalize on what he called the "curative powers" of Soda Creek's mineral spring water. The resort included a hotel, tennis courts, croquet course, garden and bowling alley. The hotel later burned and the property was acquired by the state of Oregon in 1940.
commons.editorial_reason: Generic snowy landscape; the description only gives historical visitation and no visible Kalapuya culture.

commons.title: Dedication ceremony (11196097115).jpg
commons.description: Speakers at the community celebration — emceed by ODOT Area Manager Frannie Brindle (standing) — included Oregon Rep. Nancy Nathanson, the mayors of Eugene and Springfield, and Kalapuya elder Esther Stutzman, among others. The ceremony commemorated the completion of the landmark bridge and honored the Eugene and Springfield communities for their involvement and support throughout the bridge’s construction.
commons.editorial_reason: Modern ceremony scene with ordinary contemporary clothing; no visible Kalapuya cultural dress, craft, or performance.

commons.title: Stopping by "The River" (9468828496).jpg
commons.description: On Aug. 3, the communities of Eugene and Springfield celebrated the opening of the Whilamut Passage Bridge. The event kicked off with a bike ride across the new northbound bridge for members of Kidical Mass Eugene, a group that promotes safe and fun bike rides for kids and their families. During the ride, participants posed in front of “River,” one of the bridge’s design enhancements that honors the Kalapuya tribe.
commons.editorial_reason: Modern children’s bike ride and bridge artwork; the description honors Kalapuya but the image shows no Kalapuya cultural content.
